subject: Cloud Computing
title: How AWS Became the Leader
description: Learn How AWS Became the Leader in one minute.

hook.text: AWS launched in 2006 with two services. Today it offers over 200 and earns $90 billion a year.

buildup.text: Amazon moved first, captured developers, and built a flywheel: more users meant lower prices.

discovery.text: AWS commands about 31% of the cloud market — more than Azure and Google Cloud combined.

twist.text: AWS isn't Amazon's biggest revenue source. But it is by far its biggest profit source.

climax.text: AWS subsidizes Amazon's razor-thin retail margins. Without cloud profits, Amazon looks very different.

punchline.text: A bookstore's side project became tech's most profitable division.

quiz.question: What role does AWS play in Amazon's overall business?
options: It is Amazon's biggest profit source despite not being the biggest revenue source
AWS is a small experimental division within Amazon
AWS generates revenue but has never been profitable

details.summary: AWS became the cloud leader by launching first in 2006, iterating rapidly on customer feedback, and building an unmatched breadth of services. Its culture of adding services based on customer demand, rather than top-down planning.
details.whyItMatters: AWS's path to leadership illustrates how first-mover advantage combined with relentless customer focus creates durable market dominance in platform businesses.
takeaways: AWS launched five years before serious competition
Customer-driven service expansion built the broadest catalog
Over 200 services cover virtually every cloud use case

faq.question: What was AWS's key strategic advantage?
faq.answer: AWS treated infrastructure as a product, not a cost center. While Google and Microsoft were focused on their core businesses, Amazon invested heavily in making infrastructure accessible as a service. By the time competitors launched, AWS had years of operational learning and a massive customer base.

faq.question: How many services does AWS offer?
faq.answer: AWS offers over 200 services spanning compute, storage, databases, analytics, machine learning, IoT, security, and more. The breadth means customers can find a managed service for almost any workload, reducing the need to build and operate their own solutions.
